Individual Project, DSCI 100 (80 points)¶

INSTRUCTIONS¶

Complete the following questions individually using the provided data set. When prompted, fill out the cells with your code (in code cells) or text (in text cells) to answer the question. The cells will have "%%% EDIT THIS MARKDOWN CELL %%%" or "### EDIT THIS CODE CELL ###" prompting you to overwrite the contents of the cell with your answer.

Your report must be fully reproducible, and run without error by itself with no other files.

REFERENCES¶

Students are required to use methods discussed in DSCI 100 for the project report. However, there may be some stages where you wish to research on how to handle "messy" data, including outliers, missing data, etc. If you refer to anything beyond DSCI 100, please include a link to the reference at the end of this report. It does not need to be a "formal" reference like an academic paper or website, you can link to blog posts or websites like StackExchange if they are relevant to your analysis.

This analysis is based on methods learned in DSCI 100, so you should have all of the tools you need to write this code from scratch. You may use Generative AI (i.e., ChatGPT, Gemini, etc) as an "advanced search engine" (i.e., to help de-bug code).You cannot use it to generate code or text on the report. Part 1: The Data (2 points)¶

We will be exploring a data set on Women's March Madness (Basketball). This adapted data set contains historical records of every NCAA Division I Women’s Basketball Tournament appearance since the tournament began in 1982 up until 2018. Sourced from official NCAA, the adapted data set captures tournament results across more than four decades of collegiate women’s basketball. All data is sourced from the NCAA and contains the data behind the story The Rise and Fall Of Women’s NCAA Tournament Dynasties.

The data set can be read in from the following url: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diverse-data-hub/diversedata/refs/heads/main/data-clean/womensmarchmadness.csv

To help you with the analysis, here is a table of descriptions of each of the variables present in the model.

Variable Description
year Year
school School Name
seed Seed. The 0 seeding designation in 1983 notes the eight teams that played an opening-round game to become the No. 8 seed in each region.
conference Conference
conf_wins Conference Wins
conf_losses Conference Losses
conf_wins_pct Conference Win Percentage
conf_rank Place in Conference
division Conference Division
reg_wins Regional Wins
reg_losses Regional Losses
reg_wins_pct Regional Win Percentage
bid Whether the school qualified with an automatic bid (by winning its conference or conference tournament) or an at-large bid. [‘at-large’, ‘auto’]
first_game_at_home Whether the school played its first-round tournament games on its home court. [‘Y’, ‘N’]
tourney_wins Tourney Wins
tourney_losses Tourney Losses
tourney_finish Ordered categories: [‘opening_round_loss’ < ‘first_round_loss’ < ‘second_round_loss’ < ‘top_16_loss’ < ‘top_8_loss’ < ‘top_4_loss’ < ‘top_2_loss’ < ‘champ’]
total_wins Total Wins
total_losses Total Losses
total_wins_pct Total Win Percentage

Part 5: Analysis (34 points)¶

In this section, you will describe your data analysis and perform it.

Task 5.1 Plan out your analysis (10 points)¶

Propose a method that was covered in class that would be appropriate to use to answer your research question. You only need to build one model with one set of predictors in this section. Write a paragraph that explains the choice of method, and be sure to answer the following questions:

  • What method do you plan to use?
  • Why is this method appropriate?
  • What are the potential limitations or weaknesses of the method selected?
  • How are you going to process the data to apply the model? For example: Are you splitting the data? How? How many splits? What proportions will you use for the splits? At what stage will you split? Will there be a validation set? Will you use cross validation?
  • How will you assess the performance of the model? Explain why the performance metric(s) chosen ise appropriate.

You answer should be around 250 words or less.

To predict whether a team will win or lose their opening tournament game based on regular-season performance and seed, a multivariable linear regression model will be used. It is appropriate since the model is something learned in course as well the determined coefficients are likely to be straightforward to interpret by showing a percentage value that shows the probability increase or decrease of winning the opening game. The model is however limited by the use of a linear straight line fit since it can predict negative/out-of-bound values. To process our data, an 80/20 train-test split will be conducted. 80% will be used to train the model and 20% will be used to test the model after it is complete. This split will be made after creating the target variable (won_first_game) and removing missing rows, but before fitting the linear model. Additionally, a 5-fold cross-validation will be conducted on the training set to evaluate the model's stability of predictions across different subsets of data. Lastly, an RMSE will be collected to calculate the average squared difference error between the actual outcomes and the model's numeric predictions. As well, a confusion matrix will be used to calculate the overall classification accuracy of the model. These performance assessment techniques will help evaluate how close the predicted win probabilities are to true outcomes and if it can correctly predict wins/losses of the teams participating.

    mutate( #Tourney wins is originally a factor so numerify it 
            won_first_game = if_else(as.numeric(as.character(tourney_wins)) >= 1, 1, 0) 
        #tourney_wins where 1 = won first game, 0 = lost first game
        ) |> 
    select(#Selects the predictors to use in the model 
        won_first_game, 
        seed, 
        reg_wins_pct, 
        conf_wins_pct, 
        conf_rank
        ) |> 
    drop_na() #drop rows with missing values
head(clean_model) #double checking by pulling up the first 6

clean_split <- initial_split(clean_model, prop = 0.8, strata = won_first_game)
train_data <- training(clean_split) #splits the data 80/20 for training/testing 
test_data <- testing(clean_split) 
lm_recipe <- recipe( #sets the recipe to predict first game win from predictors
    won_first_game ~ seed + reg_wins_pct + conf_wins_pct + conf_rank, 
    data = train_data #using training data set to train the model
    )
lm_spec <- linear_reg() |> #making the model specification for linear regression model
    set_engine("lm") |> 
    set_mode("regression") 
lm_workflow <- workflow() |> #workflow to fit the data with the model and recipe
    add_recipe(lm_recipe) |> 
    add_model(lm_spec)
cv_folds <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 5, strata = won_first_game) #make 5 fold cross 
cv_results <- lm_workflow |> #using the lm_workflow to then fit resamples of it
    fit_resamples(resamples = cv_folds) #checking resamples 
collect_metrics(cv_results) #collecting the results of it by the rmse and rsq - rmse is only relevant one

#add in the 5-fold validation cross and then run with test data to see the confusion matrix after
lm_fit <- lm_workflow |> #fitting workflow to training data
    fit(data = train_data) 
lm_preds <- lm_fit |> #uses the fit data to predict for test data
    predict(test_data) |> #predicting by using test data that we saved aside until now

lm_test_results <- lm_preds |> #now making the results for rmse

Task 5.3 Create a Visualization or Table of the Results of your Analysis (4 points)¶

  • Create a visualization or table that is relevant to the results of your analysis (comment your code throughout so that it is easy to follow).
  • Describe what this visualization or table is showing, and why it is important to the analysis (approx 150 words or less).

This table shows the RMSE values from the training set when a 5-fold cross-validation is performed, while comparing it to the RMSE when using the testing set, showing a difference of ~0.013. Additionally, it is also shows the predictions vs actual wins/losses that the model predicts accurately and inaccurately. The model accurately predicts 330 out of the 407 teams in the test set that either won their first game or lost it (81.1% accuracy). This data is important to the analysis as it shows the model's prediction error stays consistent on unseen tournament data (based on RMSE) and that regular season performance and seed can separate most opening-round winners from losers. It also leaves room to examine where the linear model limits occur and how false predictions can upset it.

Part 6: Discuss your Results (10 points)¶

In this section, you will discuss some interesting findings from your analysis in Part 5

Task 6.1: Discuss your findings (10 points)¶

In 1 to 2 paragraphs (approx. 300 words or less):

  • Summarize what you found from the analysis in Part 5, in relation to your research question of interest.
  • The data science workflow is an iterative process. Discuss if at any point you had to adjust your analysis plan based on the results.
  • Discuss whether this is what you expected, or if anything was surprising.
  • Discuss the impact of the results, and what future questions this could lead to.

By using a multivariable linear regression model and setting up a 5-fold cross-validation and test set confusion matrix, the analysis highlighted the seed and regular season performance such as first game wins, conference win percentages, and conference rankings to reliably predict opening tournament game outcomes. With a 0.5 threshold on the test set, the model accomplished an accuracy of 81.1% by correctly classifying 330 of 407 teams with 41 false wins (actual = 0, predicted = 1) and 36 false losses (actual = 1, predicted = 0). It also maintained a consistent error during the 5-fold cross-validation (0.3764 RMSE) and test evaluation (0.3632 RMSE) with only a difference of ~0.013 (held up when using unseen data on the test set). Since the model performed reliably and matched what I originally planned, I did not need to change my research question or analysis workflow based on the observed results. Overall, the model was able to predict first game outcomes that matched my expectations and research question, however I was surprised that the accuracy of the model was greater than 75% and held steadily on unseen test data. Additionally, these results and potentially the model analysis can help inform bracket picks or highlight where tournament losses deviate from regular-season trends, although a linear model cannot guarantee a "perfect bracket" since it produces continuous scores and doesn't take upsets into account often. In the future, I could explore non-linear or classification models and extend predictions beyond first round games to determine which specific team will advance into further rounds of the tournament and hopefully on to win it all. Other areas to explore could be to determine whether a team is more likely to win their first game if played at home, or predicting how many points a team will get by the end of the season based on their last season's statistics.
